entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Adandozan was a king of the Kingdom of Dahomey, in present-day Benin, from 1797 until 1818, reigning during a pivotal period of African history marked by industrial expansion and imperial encroachment from European powers. His rule ended with a coup d'état orchestrated by his brother Ghezo, who subsequently erased Adandozan from the official historical records of Dahomey, resulting in substantial uncertainty and gaps in contemporary understanding of many aspects of his life, legacy, and reign.

Adandozan ascended to the throne in 1797 following the death of his father Agonglo, but he was remarkably young at the time of succession. Consequently, a regent was appointed to exercise executive authority and oversee the affairs of the kingdom until 1804, when Adandozan assumed direct control of governance. His reign inherited the severe economic challenges that had plagued the administrations of both his father Agonglo and his grandfather Kpengla, characterized by declining revenues and fiscal instability.

Faced with these mounting economic pressures, Adandozan pursued reformist policies aimed at reducing the kingdom's dependence on the slave trade, seeking to diminish European commercial influence and mitigate the social upheaval caused by the lucrative but destabilizing slave trade economy. When these initial reform efforts proved insufficient, Adandozan shifted his policy focus toward comprehensive economic restructuring, prioritizing the development of agriculture as an alternative foundation for Dahomey's prosperity and long-term stability. His reign represents a significant moment in West African history, standing at the intersection of dynastic succession, sovereign authority traditions, and the broader transformations of the modern era marked by industrialization and imperial expansion.
